questions.q: If every report on a server is running slowly, what's the most likely category of fix?
options: Removing all expressions from every report
Infrastructure — hardware, separating the report server from its database, or a scale-out deployment
Disabling caching on every report
Rewriting every report's dataset queries individually
questions.explain: When the slowness is server-wide rather than tied to one report, the cause is almost always infrastructure, not any single report's design.

questions.q: Before reaching for caching or a snapshot on a slow report, what should you check first?
options: Whether the report uses Report Builder instead of SSDT
Whether the dataset query is filtering, sorting, and aggregating at the data source instead of inside the report
Whether the report has a title on the title slide
Whether the report is stored in a subfolder instead of the Home folder
questions.explain: Caching and snapshots multiply the benefit of an efficient query — they don't fix an inefficient one. Query tuning comes first.

questions.q: Why does a snapshot help a report with a genuinely slow underlying query more than caching alone?
options: Snapshots use a different, faster query engine than live reports
A snapshot automatically rewrites the query to be faster
Caching is only available for reports with no parameters at all
Caching still makes the very first requester pay the full query cost; a snapshot runs on its own schedule and never makes a live user wait for it
questions.explain: A cached report still processes fully on the first request; a snapshot is captured ahead of time on its own schedule, so no live viewer ever triggers the slow query.

questions.q: What's the concern with a heavy nested expression repeated across five textboxes in a large table?
options: It gets re-evaluated once per relevant scope — potentially once per row in a repeating table — adding real rendering time
Report Builder and SSDT store expressions differently, so this would break on deployment
SSRS expressions can only be used in the title slide, so this would cause an error
Expressions are cached automatically, so this pattern has no real performance cost
questions.explain: Expressions evaluate at render time; a heavy expression repeated per row in a table or matrix adds up fast — often better moved into a calculated field.

questions.q: How can you tell whether a performance change actually helped, rather than just feeling faster?
options: Check the RDL file's XML for a performance rating field
Ask a few users whether the report feels snappier
Check the report server's execution log for processing time before and after the change
Assume any caching change is automatically an improvement
questions.explain: The execution log records how long each report actually took to process, giving you a real before-and-after number instead of a guess.
